When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, promptly wrote the address of the county archive across the lid in black marker.

Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street and keeps its piano as it was in the early years, telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere, who came the next week. The archivist found the reel sound and supple, though film that old, she said, can catch fire near a hot lamp. When she asked for an empty spool, Brask sent one across the lobby with a gentle underhand pitch. Colm, holding a frame to the window, was the first to recognize the street and place it in town: their grandfather’s hardware sign hung over a doorway.

The archive’s laboratory had a waiting list, and the delay stretched through the summer while a collector in the city wrote twice offering to buy it. The archive paid for the copy out of its own money, so Brask had only the waiting to bear.

Brask wanted live music, and the only person in Carrow who had ever played for silent films was Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist. She had not set foot in the building in forty years. Ines and Colm argued with Brask that a recording would do, but he called at Mabel’s house three evenings running, and on the fourth she came down and asked him to run the copy for her privately while she found the music.

In October the copy was screened at the Lantern to a full house, and the reel showed the town exactly what the pencilled lid had promised. The original stayed in Dunmere, where everyone agreed it belonged. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She told him she would, as long as the original reel stayed locked in the archive’s vault and was never carried into the Lantern’s hot little booth.

Odile had sealed the lid with a ring of pitch, and Halloway softened it with a warm iron before she could lift it. The reel beneath had shrunk, and its outer turns were already crumbling into brown dust. She drove it back to the archive in a chilled box.

Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist, knew how it had come to be in the attic. Mabel has played for every silent show at the Lantern since she was a girl, and she remembered Odile’s father, who ran the projector there a century ago, carrying a canister home under his coat on the night he gave up the job.

The rescue took Halloway four months. She eased the reel open turn by turn and copied it frame by frame onto safety film, and the archive paid for the work out of its own money. The delay cost Colm his sale, since the collector wanted a reel that could still run; Colm argued with Halloway for a week and then let it go.

In October Brask ran the copy privately for Mabel, and she was the first to recognize the street, naming the town bakery’s awning. A week later the copy was screened at the Lantern to a full house, and the reel showed the town exactly what the pencilled lid had promised, while the original stayed in Dunmere, where it belonged. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She said she would, and asked him to print Wren Halloway’s name on the poster in letters larger than her own.

passage:
When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, carried it down the hill that evening to Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist, who has played for its silent nights since she was a girl, and brought it home unopened, since she owned no projector.

Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street, telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere, who came the next week. Ines showed her where the canister had lain, under the steep pitch of the roof, and the archivist found the reel sound and supple. Holding a frame up to the window, Halloway was the first to recognize the street and place it in town: the bakery awning was on half the Carrow postcards she had catalogued.

In the Lantern’s early years, Brask told her, every seat was taken on Saturdays, and a reel of the town’s own fair would have run within the week. These days the hall fills only on Mabel’s silent nights, and the cinema has lost money for a decade.

The archive’s laboratory would copy the reel for a fee, and the Lantern could barely pay for heat. A collector in the city wrote offering three times the cost, and Colm left the letter unanswered. The town council argued for a month over a grant and gave nothing. So Brask raised the money himself, selling seats months ahead and auctioning its old brass ticket booth, and after a short delay the copy was made. The original went to the archive, where Ines had always said it belonged.

In October the copy was screened at the Lantern to a full house, and the reel showed the town exactly what the pencilled lid had promised. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She said she would, and then played the fair-day march again at double speed, laughing as the children in the front row stamped to keep up.

When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, took the canister from her hands, climbed back up the ladder and set it behind the chimney exactly where it had been.

Ines brought it down the next morning, and they argued about it all summer. At last she took it to Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street and keeps its piano as it was in the early years, and he telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere. Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist, who has played for its silent nights since she was a girl, was at the piano, and after a few chords she said its pitch had sagged so far that it needed a tuner.

Halloway unwound a few feet in the lobby, and it was Brask who placed the scene. Holding a frame to the window, he matched the striped awning in one corner to the one still over the bakery across the road. It had been filmed from the Lantern’s roof, looking down on their own town.

The archivist found the reel sound and supple, and after a short delay the archive made a copy, for a fee Ines paid herself. A collector in the city offered to buy the original, and neither answered. Colm still argued that a family film belonged in the family’s house; Ines, that it belonged to the street it showed. In September Colm agreed to let the original go to the archive if the copy came home.

In October the copy was screened at the Lantern to a full house, and the reel showed the town exactly what the pencilled lid had promised. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She said she would, and told him that the last time she had played to a house that full, her sister, twenty years gone now, had been sitting in the third row.

When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, telephoned Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street and keeps its piano as it was in the early years, that night to ask which Saturday was free.

Brask telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere, who came the next week. The archivist found the reel sound and supple, and Ines, holding a frame to the window, was the first to recognize the street and place it in town: the striped awning of the bakery where she had once worked. Colm read out a letter from a collector in the city that promised a fair price and a cold vault, and then hurried off to referee a match on the school pitch.

Halloway wanted the original locked in the archive before it was run anywhere; a reel that old, she said, belonged where it could be kept cold. Colm wanted the town to see it first, on the Lantern’s screen, where it would have played a century ago. They argued across the lobby for an hour while Brask swept around them.

The archive made the copy after a short delay, and Brask paid for it from the Lantern’s takings. Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist, who has played for its silent nights since she was a girl, worked out a fair-day march for it, and Brask put up posters promising a fair.

But when the copy was screened at the Lantern in October, the oldest people in the house began to murmur, and the town discovered what the reel really showed. The crowd on Ferry Street was carrying chairs through water a foot deep: it was the morning after the great flood, filed in the wrong tin. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She said she would, but only after he took down every poster in Carrow, because it was wrong to keep selling tickets to a fair the reel had never shown.
